react_result.final_narrative_text: The nine differentially abundant metabolites form a tightly coordinated tryptophan-centered signature across three independent enrichment paradigms. Tryptophan metabolism (KEGG:hsa00380 / map00380) achieves rank #1 consensus: it is the top hit in the RaMP multi-DB ORA (FDR = 8.86 × 10⁻¹⁹, 7 of 54 pathway members), the top hit in the MetaboAnalystR KEGG-specific PSEA (p = 5.41 × 10⁻⁹, 6 of 41), and the top hit in the Mummichog empirical-compound network analysis (p = 3.36 × 10⁻⁴, 8 of 17). The seven core driver metabolites are L-tryptophan, indoleacetaldehyde, tryptamine, serotonin, melatonin, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, and quinolinic acid — all confirmed as pathway members by the enrichment results' compound rosters. A second biological layer emerges in the Reactome "Serotonin and melatonin biosynthesis" pathway (REACT:R-HSA-209931, FDR = 2.02 × 10⁻⁸), where L-tryptophan is converted first to serotonin and then to melatonin via arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT). The kynurenine-branch driver metabolites — 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid and quinolinic acid — appear in the RaMP "Tryptophan catabolism leading to NAD+ production" (WP:WP4210, FDR = 5.82 × 10⁻¹¹) and the "IDO metabolic pathway" (WP:WP5414, FDR = 8.38 × 10⁻⁹), reflecting the two major arms of tryptophan catabolism. The serotonin/melatonin axis therefore shows differential abundance across both its biosynthetic and degradative branches, suggesting a treatment-induced shift in tryptophan flux that simultaneously affects neuroactive amine production and NAD⁺-precursor supply. Ureidosuccinic acid (N-carbamoyl-L-aspartic acid) and O-phosphoethanolamine are peripheral: they are not tryptophan-metabolism members but map to pyrimidine metabolism (MUMM, p = 0.047) and glycerophospholipid metabolism (MUMM), respectively.

react_result.final_narrative_text: The nine differentially abundant metabolites show a convergent tryptophan-metabolism signal across three independent enrichment paradigms (RaMP multi-DB ORA, Mummichog m/z network, and Reactome ORA). The KEGG map00380 Tryptophan metabolism pathway is the top-ranked RaMP hit (FDR = 8.86e-19) and contains seven of the nine input metabolites. The Mummichog empirical-compound network analysis identifies tryptophan metabolism as the top pathway (p = 0.000168, 16 of 17 matched metabolites). The WikiPathways WP:WP4210 Tryptophan catabolism leading to NAD+ production (FDR = 5.82e-11) captures the kynurenine-branch metabolites 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid and quinolinic acid. The Reactome R-HSA-209931 Serotonin and melatonin biosynthesis (FDR = 2.02e-08) connects the neurotransmitter arm. The four driver metabolites — L-tryptophan, serotonin, melatonin, and quinolinic acid — are detected across both biosynthetic and catabolic branches of this network. Cross-paradigm consensus on tryptophan metabolism (rank 1 in RaMP ORA, rank 1 in Mummichog, rank 8 in Reactome ORA) establishes this as the dominant biological story.

Tryptophan metabolism (KEGG:hsa00380 / map00380) achieves rank #1 consensus: it is the top hit in the RaMP multi-DB ORA (FDR = 8.86 × 10⁻¹⁹, 7 of 54 pathway members), the top hit in the MetaboAnalystR KEGG-specific PSEA (p = 5.41 × 10⁻⁹, 6 of 41), and the top hit in the Mummichog empirical-compound network analysis (p = 3.36 × 10⁻⁴, 8 of 17). The seven core driver metabolites are L-tryptophan, indoleacetaldehyde, tryptamine, serotonin, melatonin, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, and quinolinic acid — all confirmed as pathway members by the enrichment results' compound rosters. A second biological layer emerges in the Reactome "Serotonin and melatonin biosynthesis" pathway (REACT:R-HSA-209931, FDR = 2.02 × 10⁻⁸), where L-tryptophan is converted first to serotonin and then to melatonin via arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT). The kynurenine-branch driver metabolites — 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid and quinolinic acid — appear in the RaMP "Tryptophan catabolism leading to NAD+ production" (WP:WP4210, FDR = 5.82 × 10⁻¹¹) and the "IDO metabolic pathway" (WP:WP5414, FDR = 8.38 × 10⁻⁹), reflecting the two major arms of tryptophan catabolism. The serotonin/melatonin axis therefore shows differential abundance across both its biosynthetic and degradative branches, suggesting a treatment-induced shift in tryptophan flux that simultaneously affects neuroactive amine production and NAD⁺-precursor supply. Ureidosuccinic acid (N-carbamoyl-L-aspartic acid) and O-phosphoethanolamine are peripheral: they are not tryptophan-metabolism members but map to pyrimidine metabolism (MUMM, p = 0.047) and glycerophospholipid metabolism (MUMM), respectively.
